issues.legal_issue: Continued occupation after a lawful entry does not constitute criminal trespass without the requisite criminal intent, and a complaint alleging only a civil possession dispute cannot support criminal proceedings.
material_facts: The occupant was invited by the owner to live in the house and resided there peacefully during the owner's lifetime.
After the owner died, the occupant remained in the house despite a written request to vacate.

The complaint alleged that she had not vacated after notice, but did not allege the requisite intent to commit an offence, intimidate, insult or annoy a person in possession, or take unauthorised possession or make unauthorised use of the property.
The occupant could seek to justify her possession in a civil eviction proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The complaint did not make out criminal trespass; treating the essentially civil dispute as a criminal proceeding was an abuse of process, and the conviction could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code, including its amendment by U.P. Act 31 of 1961, criminal trespass requires the specified criminal intent; a trespass alone is insufficient. Section 448 provides the punishment for criminal trespass. The Court relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.criminal_trespass_prosecution_based_on_c: A criminal trespass prosecution is brought on the basis that a person continued occupying property after being asked to leave.
predicates.lawful_initial_entry: The occupant originally entered or began residing on the property with the permission of a person entitled to allow it.
predicates.bona_fide_civil_possession_dispute: The occupant may have a civil basis for claiming a right to remain on the property.
predicates.no_allegation_of_requisite_criminal_inte: The complaint does not allege that the occupant acted with the intent required to make the occupation criminal.

issues.definition: When a criminal trespass prosecution is based on continued occupation following a lawful entry or amid a genuine civil possession dispute, and the complaint does not allege the requisite criminal intent, the occupation is not criminal trespass and the prosecution is an abuse of process.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a magistrate's conviction is appealable when the magistrate imposes a fine and also directs the convicted person to vacate the property.
material_facts: The Magistrate imposed a fine and also directed the occupant to vacate the premises within two months.
The Sessions Judge allowed the occupant's appeal, but the High Court held that the appeal was incompetent because a fine had been imposed.
issues.conclusion: The appeal to the Sessions Judge was competent and maintainable because the order included a direction to vacate the premises, purportedly under Section 456 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished an order imposing only a fine, for which revision rather than appeal would be competent, from an order that also directs the person to vacate property. The latter direction, purportedly made under Section 456 of the Criminal Procedure Code, made the order appealable. The Court considered but rejected the High Court's view concerning Section 401(5) of that Code. It relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.appeal_from_magistrate_conviction: A person convicted by a magistrate challenges the conviction in an appellate court.
predicates.magistrate_imposed_fine: The magistrate imposed a fine as part of the order.
predicates.magistrate_order_includes_direction_to_v: The magistrate's order also directs the convicted person to leave the property.

issues.definition: An appeal from a magistrate's conviction is maintainable when the magistrate imposed a fine and also directed the convicted person to vacate property.
